title: New Zealand Hotels Book Out Two Years Before Historic Solar Eclipse
excerpt: Accommodation across the South Island is filling fast ahead of the July 2028 total solar eclipse — the first to cross this part of New Zealand in more than 860 years.
body:
• Hotels in Dunedin and Queenstown are already fully booked or filling rapidly for the July 22, 2028 total solar eclipse — still two years away.
  • The eclipse will be the first total solar eclipse visible in New Zealand's South Island since 1163, with up to 50,000 visitors expected in Dunedin alone.
  • The path of totality crosses the Indian Ocean, Sydney, and New Zealand's South Island — offering Indian travellers a rare chance to combine Australia and NZ in one eclipse trip.
  • Travel experts recommend securing accommodation and flights by late 2026 or early 2027, as winter ski season compounds demand in Queenstown.

Two years out from one of the most anticipated celestial events in the Southern Hemisphere, hotels across New Zealand's South Island are already running dry. The total solar eclipse of July 22, 2028 — the first to cross this part of the country in more than 860 years — has triggered an accommodation scramble that tourism operators say is unlike anything they have seen.

An 860-Year Wait Ends in Dunedin

The centre line of the moon's shadow will pass directly through Dunedin, delivering 2 minutes and 51 seconds of totality beginning at 4:17 pm local time, according to timeanddate.com. Queenstown, further west along the path, will see an even longer 2 minutes and 54 seconds of darkness starting at 4:16 pm.

The last time a total solar eclipse was visible in this part of New Zealand was in 1163 — centuries before Dunedin was even established. The most recent total eclipse anywhere in the country was in 1965, and that was visible only in a small sliver of Northland.

Dunedin Leisure Lodge, one of the city's prominent hotels sitting squarely in the totality zone, is already fully booked for eclipse dates and has moved to a waitlist system. Its sister property, Distinction Dunedin Hotel, is offering three-night eclipse packages at NZ$399 per night with a minimum stay requirement and a December 2027 payment deadline — a sign of just how far ahead the industry is planning.

"The path of the eclipse starts in the Indian Ocean and crosses through central Australia, just north of Alice Springs, then goes through Sydney, and then it goes through just north of Milford Sound and Queenstown, and on through Central Otago to Dunedin."

— Warren Hurley, Dunedin Astronomical Society

50,000 Eclipse Chasers Expected

An estimated 50,000 people are expected to descend on Dunedin for the event, according to projections cited by the Distinction Hotels group and local tourism bodies. For a city with a resident population of roughly 130,000, the influx represents a significant logistical challenge.

Otago Museum director and astronomer Dr Ian Griffin, who has chased eclipses from Mexico to Pitcairn Island, described a total solar eclipse as "the most beautiful natural phenomenon on earth." Griffin is so committed to witnessing this one from home that he bought his house a decade ago specifically because it sits on the eclipse's centre line.

"I bought a house 10 years ago right on the centreline of the eclipse and I intend to be sitting on my deck enjoying my view of the eclipse setting over the hills surrounding Dunedin and I really can't wait."

— Dr Ian Griffin, Director, Otago Museum

Dunedin is also planning a Festival of Astronomy around the eclipse, timed to coincide with Matariki, the Māori New Year celebration tied to a cluster of stars. International tour operators are already packaging multi-day itineraries: New Scientist's seven-day South Island eclipse tour, priced at £5,149 per person, includes stargazing in the Aoraki Mackenzie International Dark Sky Reserve and guided astronomy talks.

A Trans-Tasman Eclipse Trail

What makes this eclipse unusual is the breadth of its path. Dubbed the "Great Australasian Eclipse" by some media outlets, the shadow will first touch land in Western Australia's Kimberley region, sweep southeast through the Northern Territory and Queensland, then pass directly over Sydney — which hasn't seen a total eclipse since 1857. After crossing the Tasman Sea, it reaches New Zealand's South Island from Milford Sound through to Dunedin.

For Indian travellers, this geography is convenient. Sydney and Queenstown are already popular destinations, and the eclipse offers a compelling reason to combine both into a single trip. The path's origin in the Indian Ocean also means partial eclipses will be visible across parts of Southeast Asia and Indonesia.

Dr Griffin noted that if skies are clear in New Zealand, the setting would produce a once-in-a-lifetime photograph. "If you're in Milford Sound the sun will be setting behind Mitre Peak — eclipsed, and that really will be a picture for the ages," he told RNZ.

Why Booking Now Matters

Travel experts are urging prospective visitors not to wait. Discover New Zealand, a specialist travel advisory, warns that accommodation in Dunedin, Queenstown, Aoraki Mount Cook, and Lake Tekapo is inherently limited compared with major cities. Eclipse travel compounds the problem because everyone needs to be in the same narrow corridor on the same date.

July is also New Zealand's winter, and Queenstown's ski season already absorbs much of the region's hotel capacity. Rental cars, domestic flights into Christchurch and Queenstown, and guided tours are all expected to tighten well before 2028.

The precedent from the United States is instructive. During the April 2024 total eclipse across North America, hotel bookings along the path of totality surged 800 percent compared with the previous year, according to Choice Hotels data reported by Nasdaq. Officials in Niagara Falls, which sat directly in the path, declared a state of emergency to manage crowds.

New Zealand's South Island, with far fewer hotel rooms and a fraction of the transport infrastructure, faces an even steeper capacity challenge. For anyone planning to witness the eclipse from Dunedin or Queenstown, the window to secure a room is closing fast.
